column4: The ayah moves from fear of injustice toward orphans to marrying two, three, or four, then restricts the hearer to one if justice is feared; orphan vulnerability, plurality, and the ethical boundary of the single meet in one formulation.
Zechariah prays, “Do not leave me single,” using فَرْدًا for a human being who seeks the addition of an heir rather than final isolation.
God answers Zechariah, grants him John, and makes his wife fit for him; this ayah supplies the restored family relation requested by the “do not leave me single” of 21:89.

God tells the messenger to leave Him with the person He created وَحِيدًا, after which the passage lists the wealth and sons added to that original solitude; created singleness, additions, and punishment form one arc.
At the upheaval of the last day, the souls are paired, وَإِذَا ٱلنُّفُوسُ زُوِّجَتْ; this directly complements the section’s single soul being joined to a company at the end.

The promise that God will not يَتِرَكُمْ your deeds uses the source root و ت ر in its different verbal sense, “deprive or leave deficient”; it lets witr evoke not only being one but being left lacking.
After named torments, the condemned receive other punishments “of the same kind, in pairs”; likeness, multiplicity by pairs, and punishment converge in a single description.
The community is commanded to marry the unmarried among them and the righteous among its male and female servants, turning socially unpaired people into pairs through communal action.

God will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him; this two-direction divine-human relation is a close nonlexical parallel to “pleased with them and pleased with Him,” and it describes a whole faithful community.
God, His messenger, and the believing worshippers are named as the believers’ allies; this relation explains the attachment through which 5:56 calls them God’s party.
The righteous enter lasting gardens together with the righteous among parents, spouses, and descendants, making garden-entry the reunion of a person with an accepted community.
The angels ask God to admit the repentant and the righteous among their parents, spouses, and descendants into Eden, explicitly making admission collective across family relations.
Believers’ faithful descendants are joined to them in the Garden without reducing anyone’s earned reward; أَلْحَقْنَا بِهِمْ makes blessed attachment itself the gift.

The oppressed men, women, and children ask for a protector and helper, while believers are summoned to fight for them; this enacts the section’s secondary sense of joining another as supporter and petitioner.
Believing men and women are أَوْلِيَآءُ بَعْضٍ, supporters of one another, so the faithful community is defined by the mutual attachment withheld from the orphan in the section.
Believers are declared brothers and ordered to reconcile their brothers; it generalizes the “orphans are your brothers” relation into the constitutive bond of the believing community.
The command كُونُوا۟ مَعَ ٱلصَّٰدِقِينَ tells the God-conscious to place themselves with a truthful company, a present ethical counterpart to final entry among God’s servants.
The believers ask to have their sins forgiven and to die مَعَ ٱلْأَبْرَارِ, imagining death as joining the righteous rather than arriving without a company.
Abraham, one person, is called an أُمَّةً obedient to God; the ayah collapses the apparent opposition between an individual and a whole faithful community.
إِنَّ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أُمَّتُكُمْ أُمَّةً وَٰحِدَةً describes a many-person community as one and joins that unity to worship of the one Lord.
The repeated declaration that the community is أُمَّةً وَٰحِدَةً makes collective belonging and oneness compatible rather than opposed.
The likeness of Jesus before God is explicitly the likeness of Adam; مَثَلَ ... كَمَثَلِ sets two extraordinary created persons as counterparts while their shared Creator remains beyond comparison.
God subjects the one who turns away to ٱلْعَذَابَ ٱلْأَكْبَرَ, presenting His punishment as the greatest and thus directly supporting the section’s claim that no punisher matches Him.
God is Lord of the two easts and the two wests; the doubled cosmic directions make the created world legible through paired extremities under one Lord.
Each of the two gardens contains two kinds of every fruit, so a paired garden holds repeated fruit-pairs within it.
The angels have wings in twos, threes, and fours; a numerical series that includes even and odd is embodied in created heavenly messengers while increase remains God’s act.
Satan summons his party to become companions of the Blaze; this is the opposing destination of a party to the soul’s entry among God’s servants.
The wrongdoers are gathered with their counterparts and what they worshipped; judgment supplies a punitive company, reversing the blessed admission among righteous servants.
Aggression may be answered only “with the like of” what was inflicted; ordinary human retaliation is bounded by a matching counterpart, unlike the unmatched divine punishment in the section.
The recompense of an evil is one like it, making equivalence the rule of measured requital and thereby a boundary around the section’s unequalled final punishment.
If believers retaliate, they must do so only to the like of what they suffered; human punishment has an equal measure even where God’s punishment has no equal agent.
The injured person first responds with the like of what was inflicted and is then wronged again; the ayah distinguishes measured equivalence from renewed excess.
Whoever does evil is recompensed only with its like, while righteous believers enter the Garden; matched requital and gracious admission are set side by side.
The recompense of an evil is an evil like it, but pardon and reconciliation are better; equivalence is a ceiling for human response rather than the final word.
Rain brings forth diverse أَزْوَٰجًا of plants; here “pairs” can also carry the sense of kinds, expanding the section’s numerical image into created botanical diversity.
The revived earth grows every beautiful pair or kind, placing paired growth inside the proof of resurrection.
The earth produces every noble pair or kind; the repeated formula makes created pairing visible in abundance rather than isolation.
God scatters creatures through the earth and grows every noble pair or kind, linking multiplicity and pairing to His ordering creation.
The spread earth produces every beautiful pair or kind, and the next ayah makes this ordered abundance a reminder for the returning servant.
Those unable to marry must remain chaste until God enriches them; this qualifies 24:32 by recognizing that the socially unpaired state can persist under divine provision.
The messenger is told to keep himself patiently with those who call on their Lord and not turn his eyes away from them, making steadfast companionship an explicit command.
Holding together to God’s rope and refusing division turns former enemies into brothers, describing the act by which separate people become one protected community.
God’s righteous servants inherit the earth, giving عِبَادِى a collective promise and a shared destination.
“My servants” are defined as a protected group over whom Satan has no authority, except those who follow him; belonging carries a real boundary.
God again tells Satan that he has no authority over “My servants,” while divine guardianship suffices for that community.
At resurrection people become three أَزْوَٰجًا, where the word means classes rather than two-member pairs; this different Quranic use shows that a “pair/kind” can name a whole company.
Pharaoh’s magicians are told to assemble their plan and come in a row, making صف a coordinated human formation before the section’s angelic rows.
Choking food and painful punishment follow the shackles and Blaze of 73:12, completing that ayah’s divine restraint scene with what the bonds lead to.
After 40:71 places collars and chains on the condemned, this ayah says they are dragged into boiling water and then burned, supplying the destination of those bonds.
The person who fears standing before his Lord receives two gardens; paired reward answers an individual stance before God.
The people of the Garden recline in shade together with their spouses, showing blessed pairing within the final community.
The messenger says no one can protect him from God and he can find no refuge besides Him, a direct statement of how every merely created supporter fails before divine judgment.
The Garden companions are likened to protected pearls in the plural; this may weakly contrast with the source dictionary’s singular “orphan pearl,” whose rarity rests on having no peer.

Serving youths are likened to well-protected pearls, again presenting a company of pearl-like figures rather than the lexicon’s single peerless “orphan pearl”; the link is limited to that dictionary illustration.
